common_name: Dam B Wisteria (Blue-Flowered Texas Native Wisteria)

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy, permanent trellis, arbor, or pergola; give Dam B three growing seasons of consistent watering to establish before expecting it to shrug off heat, drought, and cold.

directions: Dam B is a named selection of the American native wisteria discovered by legendary Texas plantsman Lynn Lowrey growing near the dam of a Southeast Texas reservoir oddly nicknamed 'Dam B,' and introduced to the nursery trade under that name. It produces light blue to lavender, finely fragrant flower racemes six to ten inches long in a strong late-May-to-June flush, with light, sporadic repeat bloom through summer and into fall on a well-established plant. Compared with the invasive Chinese and Japanese wisterias, Dam B is markedly easier to keep in bounds, sending up fewer root suckers and responding well to routine pruning. Give it full sun and well-drained soil while it establishes over its first three years; afterward it tolerates heat, drought, occasional flooding, and general garden neglect with little complaint. Prune right after the spring bloom flush to control size and shape on its permanent support.
sources: SFA Gardens (Stephen F. Austin State University) — Dave Creech

common_name: Summer Cascade Wisteria (Betty Matthews Kentucky Wisteria)

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy, permanent trellis, arbor, or pergola strong enough to carry a mature vine's weight.

directions: Sold commercially as Summer Cascade, this named selection of Kentucky wisteria (registered as 'Betty Matthews') bears fragrant, drooping flower clusters eight to twelve inches long that open dark lavender-purple and soften to a paler lavender as they age, blooming in May and June with some repeat flowering later in the season. Like other Kentucky wisteria selections it is far less rampant than Chinese or Japanese wisteria, twining without the aggressive self-seeding that makes those Asian species invasive in much of the East and Gulf South. Its exceptional cold hardiness, reliable into USDA zone 4, makes it a realistic wisteria choice for gardeners well north of where Asian wisterias thrive. The pinnately compound leaves, each with nine to fifteen leaflets, turn soft yellow-green in fall, and fuzzy brown seed pods persist into late summer. Prune immediately after the main spring bloom to control size and encourage the strongest flower bud set for the following year.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Fenway Park Boston Ivy (Golden-Leaved Boston Ivy)

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in almost any well-drained soil near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging tendrils; site in more sun for the brightest gold color and in more shade for a softer lime-green effect.

directions: Fenway Park was discovered in 1988 as a naturally occurring golden-leaved sport on the ivy-clad outfield wall of Boston's Fenway Park ballpark and was later named and released with the ballclub's permission. Its three-lobed leaves emerge bright golden yellow and hold that color best where the vine receives several hours of direct sun each day, fading to a softer chartreuse-green in deeper shade; cool autumn weather adds a rosy-red overlay to the gold before leaf drop. Like the straight species it climbs by adhesive, disc-tipped tendrils that grip brick, stone, or wood without additional support, covering walls and structures densely within a few seasons. The bright foliage makes a strong color accent against dark masonry or as a contrast planting alongside green-leaved vines, but plan for its eventual size and vigor, and prune annually to keep growth clear of windows, gutters, and roof edges.

common_name: Star Showers Virginia Creeper (Variegated Virginia Creeper)

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average to moist soil near a structure, tree, or fence; unlike the plain-green species this selection is noticeably less vigorous, so it suits smaller trellises and garden structures.

directions: Star Showers (sold under the cultivar name 'Monham') is a variegated sport of the native Virginia creeper, its five-parted palmate leaves speckled and splashed with cream and soft pink against green, giving each leaf a paint-spattered look distinct from the solid green species. New growth carries the most pink tones, and the variegated foliage shifts toward rosy pink again in winter before leaf drop. It clings to walls, fences, and tree trunks by adhesive tendril discs exactly like the species, but grows noticeably less rampantly, making it a better fit for a modestly sized arbor or trellis rather than the towering canopy coverage of an unselected Virginia creeper. It tolerates the same wide range of conditions from full sun to full shade and tough soils, and supports the same wildlife value, with berries eaten by birds and foliage serving as a larval host for native moths. Because variegation on sported selections can occasionally revert to solid green, prune out and remove any all-green shoots as soon as they appear to preserve the patterned effect.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
